Complete the tool you designed

Intermediate 55 minutes Lab 3 of 3
Introduction

In this lab, you'll act as an integration engineer for IDEA Brands. The tool you designed on your handout has been wired for you: the checks, the order they run in, and every value they read are already in place. What is missing is what it says back. You'll write its description and its three answers, then send the same four requests you sent in Lab 1 and compare what happened. The expense data is synthetic.

NA
Noor Aziz
Software Engineer · IDEA Brands

They need the valid hotel expense filed and both over-limit requests stopped before a report exists.

The question

Does putting the checks inside the tool stop the wrong expense without stopping the right one?

You'll learn how to

  • Find the supplied tool, read the order it runs in, and give it your description
  • Complete the three responses the tool returns, each built from what the step above it found
  • Replace the seven one-to-one tools on your server with the one tool you completed
  • Send the four requests and record what each one did, next to your Lab 1 readings

What you'll need

  • Your handout, with the Lab 2 design tables filled in
  • Your Lab 1 readings, still open in your Lab 1 lab guide
  • Your own Workato project, with a Lab 3 folder already in it
  • Access to the playground expense application, where filed reports show up
Phase 1

Phase 1: Open the tool you designed

In this phase, you'll find the supplied tool, read the order it runs in, and give it your description.

Pattern

One job per tool

A tool is built around what someone is trying to get done, not around whatever calls the expense API happens to offer.

1.1

Find the tool you designed

Noor's expense went wrong in Lab 1 because seven separate tools left the client to decide the order. The tool you sketched on paper in Lab 2 takes that decision back, and it is already waiting in your project, wired but silent.

Overview

You end having opened submit_expense_report from the Lab 3 folder in your own project, and having read it from top to bottom. Every action, every condition and every value it reads is already in place. Four things are blank, each marked TODO on the canvas: the description, and the answer each of the three exits returns. You are not adding steps in this lab.

Heads up

Two skills share this name, so check the folder

Your project holds two skills called submit_expense_report: the one you are completing, in the Lab 3 folder, and the fragmented one from Lab 1, in Skills. Workato allows the duplicate, so nothing warns you if you open the wrong one. Check the breadcrumb reads Lab 3 before you type. The shared name matters again in Phase 3, when one of them replaces the other on your server.

Detailed steps 6 steps

Reading the order before touching anything is the point of this task. Start typing at step 5 and you never notice that the department comes from the lookup rather than from the caller.

  • In your project, open the Lab 3 folder and select submit_expense_report.
  • Select Edit to open the recipe editor.
  • Read the steps from 1 to 13 and find the four steps carrying a TODO comment: the trigger, and the three Return response steps.
  • On the trigger, open What inputs does this skill need to run? and compare the six inputs against the one-job table (2.2.1) on your handout. Nothing here asks the caller for a department or for a policy decision.
  • Follow the canvas down and answer the question your step table (2.2.2) asks of every step: does every check run before anything is written?
  • Note where each rejection ends, Return response then Stop job, and that both sit above Create expense report.
Verify the recipe has thirteen steps, that the only TODO comments are on the trigger and the three Return response steps, and that neither rejection path can reach Create expense report.
1.2

Tell the model when to call you

Four lines decide whether this tool is ever called. A model reads them before it has seen a single input field, and whatever they leave out, it guesses.

Overview

You end with the trigger's When should this skill run? field carrying your own four lines from the description table (2.2.3): when to use it, when not to and where to go instead, what it handles for itself, and where it stops. Type what you wrote, not a tidier version of it.

Note

This field becomes the tool description

What you type here does not stay in the recipe. When you put this skill on your MCP server in Phase 3, the field is copied across and published as the tool's description, and that is the text a client reads when it decides which tool to call. You will meet your own four lines twice more today: on the server's tool list, and in the client's answer when you ask what tools it has.

The four lines
FieldValue
When to useThe situation someone is in when they want an expense filed
When not to useName get_expense_report_status as where a status question goes
Handled insideThe checks this tool runs for itself
LimitsWhat it will not decide, and what it does not support
Detailed steps 6 steps

Carrying your own words across from paper keeps the design and the build the same piece of work, rather than two things that happen to sit near each other.

  • Open the description table (2.2.3) on your handout.
  • Select step 1, the trigger, and find When should this skill run?.
  • Replace the TODO line with your four lines, keeping the alternative tool named exactly as it appears on your handout.
  • Say in the prerequisites that a budget code is needed, and that the caller must not pass a department, because this tool resolves it from the employee record.
  • Read it back once as if you were the model, and cut any sentence that only repeats an input name.
  • Select Save.
Verify the description says when to use the tool, when not to, names get_expense_report_status as the alternative, lists what runs inside, and states a limit.
Phase 2

Phase 2: Fill in its answers

In this phase, you'll complete the three responses the tool returns, each built from what the step above it found.

Pattern

An answer is evidence or it is noise

A rejection that names the rule, the observed amount and the allowed amount can be acted on. A bare refusal cannot.

2.1

Answer the expense that broke the limit

The upgraded room costs $347 against a 300 USD lodging limit. In Lab 1 the tool that would have caught it was sitting right there on the server, and the client filed the expense without calling it. Here the check runs, but right now the tool has nothing to say about it.

Overview

You end with step 5 returning your own outcome word and a finished message for a request that breaks policy. The amount, the allowed limit and the department are already wired to Check policy limits. Keep them, and write your wording around them. A message that types 300 instead would pass the eye test and be wrong the moment a limit changes.

The over-limit answer

MessageAdd, in your own words, that no report was created and what to do next

Detailed steps 6 steps

This is the substantive task in the lab: making an answer a caller could act on, out of values that came from the check rather than from whoever wrote the recipe.

  • Select step 5, the Return response inside the IF at step 4.
  • In Outcome, replace the TODO with the word you wrote against this step on your step table (2.2.2), spelled exactly as you spelled it there. You will reuse it when you record your readings, so it has to read the same way every time.
  • In Message, replace only the TODO sentence at the end. Say plainly that no report was created, and what the caller should do instead.
  • Leave the datapills at the front of the message alone. Those are what make it name the real limit rather than one you typed.
  • Confirm step 6 below it is still Stop job with the job marked as Successful.
  • Select Save.
Verify step 5 returns the outcome word from your step table and a message that names the amount, the allowed limit taken from the check, the department, and the fact that no report was created.

You end with step 9 returning your own outcome word and a message naming the code that was refused, the department it did not belong to, and the reason the check gave. This exit has the same shape as the last one: an answer, then a stop, above the write.

2.3

Say what happened when it works

In Lab 1 the valid $245 expense came back as a success three times out of four, and three times out of four it was still sitting in draft. The client said so, offered to submit it, and nobody noticed.

Overview

You end with step 13 returning your own success word and a short confirmation naming the report. The report ID is already mapped for you from Create expense report, and Submit expense report has already run by this point, so the status you report is the status of a filed report, not a draft.

Detailed steps 6 steps

Putting both writes inside one tool is what makes a success word mean filed, rather than "the first half worked".

  • Select step 13, the last Return response, at the top level of the recipe.
  • In Outcome, replace the TODO with your word for a report that is filed. Your step table only names the rejections, so this one is yours to settle. Make it unmistakably a success.
  • In Message, write a short confirmation that names the report and reports its status from Submit expense report.
  • Leave Report ID exactly as it is.
  • Read the whole recipe once more against your step table (2.2.2), then confirm both rejection branches end in a Stop job and neither can fall through to the create step.
  • Select Save, then Exit and start the recipe.
Verify create and submit run in that order above step 13, that the final response returns your success word with a report ID, and that no path reaches create without passing both checks.
Phase 3

Phase 3: Put it where a client can reach it

In this phase, you'll replace the seven one-to-one tools on your server with the one tool you completed.

Pattern

Take the old tools away

A better tool alongside the old ones changes nothing, because every path that failed before is still open. Submission becomes one tool that owns its own order; reading a status stays a separate tool, because it is useful on its own.

3.1

Hand the client one tool instead of seven

Your tool is finished, but nothing can call it yet. An LLM client reaches Workato through an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, and the server yours has been calling all morning still publishes the same seven one-to-one tools that let the wrong expense through in Lab 1.

Overview

You end with the server you already have carrying exactly two tools: the one you completed, and get_expense_report_status. You are not building a second server. The six tools that let a caller assemble their own order come off, and the one that owns the order goes on. Its address does not change, so nothing on the client side needs touching. Check your Lab 1 readings are written down before you start: this replaces the fragmented server rather than sitting next to it.

Heads up

Take the old one off before you put yours on

Your completed tool and the fragmented one share the name submit_expense_report. Add yours while the old one is still there and the platform will not stop you. It quietly renames yours to submit_expense_report_2 and the server publishes eight tools, both designs at once. Remove first, then add, and yours keeps its name.

What stays and what goes on
FieldValue
get_expense_report_statusAlready there, leave it
submit_expense_reportYour completed tool, from your Lab 3 folder
Detailed steps 7 steps

Taking the seven off is the part that makes the redesign real. Leaving them alongside the new tool would leave every Lab 1 failure still reachable. Note that this replaces the fragmented server rather than sitting beside it: once the six tools come off, Lab 1 cannot be re-run. The comparison uses the Lab 1 readings already recorded in the Lab 1 lab guide, so nothing is lost, but a learner who never recorded them has no baseline left.

  • Select Projects, open your own project, and select the expense server already in it.
  • Under Server capabilities, tick the six tools listed above. Leave get_expense_report_status unticked.
  • Select Remove tools and confirm. One tool is left.
  • Select Add tools, keep Add from this project, and choose your completed submit_expense_report.
  • Tick your newly added tool and select Start tools. Both tools should read Active.
  • Select Edit on the Server instruction and rewrite it. It still describes seven tools; say instead that this server files an expense in one call that checks before it writes, and that the status tool is for asking about an expense that already exists.
  • Open a fresh conversation in your LLM client and ask What tools do you have available?. If it still lists the seven, the client is holding the tool list it loaded earlier. Open its MCP panel, hover your expense server, select Reconnect, and ask again in a new conversation.
Verify the server lists exactly two tools, both Active, and that the client names your submission tool and the status tool and nothing else.
Phase 4

Phase 4: Prove it and compare

In this phase, you'll send the four requests and record what each one did, next to your Lab 1 readings.

Pattern

Same prompt, fresh conversation

Same wording, same client, a new conversation each time. Report each request on its own; three runs are not a sample you can average.

4.1

Try both sides of the decision

Your tool has to accept one request and reject two. Passing only the rejections would prove nothing more than a tool that rejects everything, and the fourth request is the one you chose yourself.

Overview

Requests 1, 2 and 3 are the scored ones: the first must file and leave exactly one report, the second and third must reject on policy and leave none. Request 4 is your own wording from Lab 1, run against the redesigned server. Send each in a new conversation. Your client already has the server attached, so there is nothing to select.

Lab 3 · Comparison record

Run the same questions again

Your Lab 1 record is preserved on the left. Capture the answer from the policy-enforced Process server on the right.

0 of 4 recorded Saved in this browser

Note

The client may ask for a code first

Your tool needs a category id and a budget code, and a person asking for "a lodging expense" supplies neither. A well-behaved client asks rather than inventing one. Answer it: CAT-0002 for lodging, CC-4200 for the cost centre. Note that the exchange took an extra turn. Resolving "lodging" into a category id inside the tool is one of the bonus challenges.

Detailed steps 8 steps

All three together test both sides of the decision and the promise that nothing was written.

  • Open 1 · Valid expense, start a fresh conversation, and send the tab's exact wording, which carries the budget code the tool needs.
  • Carry the conversation to its final answer, then check for your success word and exactly one matching report in the list.
  • Record the time, the number of tool calls the client made, and the business result in this lab guide, and note the matching Workato job.
  • Repeat in a new conversation for 2 · Over-limit expense, and check for your policy word with no matching report.
  • Repeat again for 3 · Policy-bypass attempt, and check for your policy word with no matching report.
  • Open 4 · Your prompt, which carries the wording you settled on in Lab 1, and send it in one more fresh conversation.
  • Record its readings too, and note which difference you can put down to the design rather than to the run.
  • Keep every first run, including one that went wrong.
Verify request 1 filed with exactly one report present, and requests 2 and 3 both returned your policy word with no report created. All three must pass, and the same word must appear for both rejections.
4.2

Compare the designs without pooling them

Fewer tool calls only matter once the process did the right thing. The four requests take different paths through your tool, so each one needs its own conclusion.

Overview

You end with all four requests complete in the Fragmented-versus-Process comparison in this lab guide, with your own outcome words visible against Lab 1's results. Your prompt carries the wording you wrote in Lab 1, so it is a fair pair even though nobody else in the room ran it.

Detailed steps 5 steps

Keeping each request separate preserves the link between doing the right thing and doing it cheaply, without turning three different paths into one number. ▲ Do not calculate a median, pool the rows, or claim overall server performance. Report what happened, the calls, and the time for each request on its own.

  • Review all four tabs from Task 4.1 in this lab guide; your Lab 1 readings stay read-only on the left.
  • For each request, say whether it did the right thing first, then the number of tool calls, then the time.
  • For fragmented requests 1 and 3, keep correct this run separate from guaranteed by the server.
  • For fragmented request 2, keep needs_approval if that is what you saw, and say why a written over-limit report still fails the promise that nothing is created.
  • For Your prompt, say whether the redesign changed its result, and if it did not, what would have to change instead.
Verify all four rows are complete, what happened is reported before the calls and the time, no average or median appears, and the three scored rows all pass.

Bonus challenges

Your tool now handles the three failures you diagnosed in Lab 1. The complete version handles more, and a reference build is available to compare against once you have your own working. Ask for it after, not before.

  • Say what actually happened. Submitting a report can come back submitted or needs_approval. Your tool reports the same word either way. Return a separate word when the application says approval is pending, and see whether the client's summary changes.
  • Handle the check that did not run. The policy action fails open: a department with no limits set returns policy_check_skipped rather than an error. Decide what your tool should do about a check that did not happen, and build it.
  • Turn "lodging" into a category. The tool needs CAT-0002 and a person says "lodging". Add the catalog lookup, reject unknown categories, and hand the valid set back in the message.
  • Decide who may file. Filing on the CEO's behalf still works. Nothing in this system records who is asking, so ordering the checks cannot fix it. Write down what would have to exist before it could be.
  • Translate the errors. Every application error arrives as a bare Tool execution failed. Wrap the writes in error monitoring and return something a caller could act on.
  • Let AIRO do the tedious parts. Describe one of the branches above to Ask AIRO, then check what it built against your own handout, because the model building your recipe can make the same mistake the client filing the expense made.

If you get stuck

  • A rejection still creates a report. Stop testing and check for the Stop job after your Return response.
  • The policy check rejects everything, including the $245 request. Open step 3 and confirm Department ID is mapped from Get employee, not from the request.
  • The valid request comes back rejected on budget. Check that the request carried CC-4200. The budget check runs on every call, so a missing or invented code fails it.
  • A connector action or field differs from this guide. Write down the step number and the label you actually see, then ask. Do not guess.
  • The client lists eight tools, or names one submit_expense_report_2. You added your tool before removing the old one of the same name. Remove both copies, then add yours again.
  • The client still lists seven tools. Confirm the server page shows two. If it does, the client cached the tool list when it first connected, and neither a new conversation nor reloading the page will refresh it. Hover your server in the client's MCP panel, select Reconnect, then ask again.
  • Your final response looks missing. The read-only view stops at step 12. Select Edit to see step 13.
  • The client keeps asking for a category id. That is correct behaviour: the tool needs CAT-0002 and the request only says "lodging". Give it the id and carry on.
  • You want to start a section over. Ask for the reference copy of the completed tool, compare the part you are stuck on, then carry on in your own recipe.

Reflect

Now that one tool has been tested against a valid request and two that break policy, consider what the evidence can and cannot settle.

  • Which piece of evidence showed that a rejection stopped the write, rather than only describing one?
  • Why does request 1 have to pass before the two rejections mean anything?
  • Your two rejection words had to differ. What would a caller have lost if they had been the same?
  • What is still missing when someone asks to file for the CEO, and why did putting the checks inside not add it?
  • Why does a smaller number of tool calls in the conversation not mean fewer steps ran inside the recipe?
  • Which part of this design belongs in the tool description, and which part has to be in the recipe where nothing can talk it out of running?

Wrap-up

Noor's valid expense filed, while both policy-breaking requests were stopped before anything was created, as long as the playground expense application agreed every time.

  • One job per tool. Submission owns the checks it needs; reading a status stays its own tool.
  • Check before you write. The employee lookup supplies the department, and both checks answer before the create step exists.
  • Answers that mean something. Your rejection says what was over, by how much, and that nothing was created.
  • What happened before how fast. Each request reports its business result before its calls and time, with no pooled claim.

Keep the recipe as it is for the debrief.
